manual.title: The Effects of Nuclear Weapons
manual.page_convention: citations use the printed page numbers of the 1977 edition; in the full scan 6852629.pdf the chapter 3 pages are printed page + 9

method.air_burst_blast: height of burst is read at the peak of each individual isobar on Fig. 3.73c (the point of maximum horizontal distance); each overpressure therefore carries its own burst height, and that height is scaled as W^(1/3)
method.ground_burst_blast: contact surface burst: the height of burst is taken as zero and the distance is read where each isobar meets the bottom edge of Fig. 3.73c (handbook p.106)
method.fireball: 110·W^0.4 ft for air bursts (2.127.1, p.70); 145·W^0.4 ft for contact surface bursts (2.127.2, p.71)
method.thermal: read directly off Fig. 7.42 (p.291) at each yield column; no scaling is applied. Fig. 7.42 is drawn for burst heights of 200·W^0.4 ft (§7.42, p.290) and for air bursts below 15,000 ft with 12-mile visibility
method.overpressure_definition: Fig. 3.73 curves are peak overpressures on the ground, i.e. they include reflection at the surface; tools quoting incident or side-on overpressure show smaller radii for the same psi

caveats: Blast heights of burst are scaled as W^(1/3), so the 1 Mt rows sit at 10,200 ft (5 psi) and 15,750 ft (1 psi). §3.73 (p.110) states the homogeneous sea-level atmosphere assumption for burst heights of 5,000 ft or less, so the 1 Mt blast rows extrapolate the handbook's assumption by a factor of 2-3. No altitude correction (§3.64-3.66) is applied; the sign of that omission is that the 1 Mt radii are understated rather than overstated.
5 psi is not printed on Fig. 3.73c. It is interpolated between the 4 and 6 psi contours at the log-pressure position 0.5503, and every 5 psi row is labelled as interpolated.
Thermal radii are slant ranges. §12.66 (p.563) notes that for ranges much greater than the burst height they may be taken as distances to ground zero, which is how they are reported here.

Thermal radii are for air bursts only. Fig. 7.42 is calculated for burst heights of 200·W^0.4 ft and the handbook's surface-burst treatment of thermal radiation (§7.41, p.290) points to a different procedure, so the ground-burst option shows blast and fireball only.

Thermal contour values on Fig. 7.42 are not printed as legible labels on the scan; they were fixed by two independent statements in the handbook (§12.66 p.563: 4.5-6 cal/cm² at 9-10 mi for 1 Mt; §7.43 p.290: 8 cal/cm² at about 7 mi). Both are reproduced within ±5% by the digitized curves.
